title: Isaiah Walks Barefoot: A Sign Against Egypt and Cush
summary: In the years when Ashdod, a Philistine city, rebelled against Assyria and looked to Egypt and Cush for rescue, God told Isaiah to take off his sackcloth and sandals and go about naked and barefoot. For three years the prophet was a living sign that the king of Assyria would lead away Egyptian and Cushite captives stripped and humiliated. Those who had made Egypt and Cush their hope would be left asking how they could possibly escape.
story: The oracles against the nations mostly speak in poetry about the future. Chapter 20 pauses for a dated prose story from the middle of Isaiah's ministry. It gives a concrete example of what chapters 18 and 19 said in poetry: Egypt and Cush cannot save anyone. The episode is a small version of the larger crisis to come, when Hezekiah is tempted to lean on Egypt against Sennacherib (chapters 30, 31, and 36). The chapter is also one of the Bible's clearest examples of a prophet acting out God's message with his own body, as Jeremiah and Ezekiel would later do.
historical:
The setting is one of the best documented events in Isaiah. Ashdod was one of the main Philistine cities on the coastal plain. Around 713 BC its king, Azuri, withheld tribute from Assyria, and Sargon II replaced him. The people of Ashdod then put a man named Yamani on the throne, who stirred up neighboring states to revolt and sought help from Egypt, by then ruled by the Kushite Twenty-Fifth Dynasty. Around 711 BC Sargon's army, led by his chief commander (Hebrew tartan, from the Assyrian title turtanu, the highest military officer), captured Ashdod. Sargon's inscriptions describe the campaign and report that Yamani fled toward Egypt and Cush, and that the Kushite king later handed him over in chains, which shows exactly how little the southern powers would risk for their small allies. Sargon's records also suggest that Judah was among the states the rebels had approached.

For centuries Sargon was known only from this verse, and some doubted he had existed. Excavations begun in the 1840s at Khorsabad in northern Iraq uncovered his capital, Dur-Sharrukin, with his palace and inscriptions, confirming the king and his campaigns. The fate Isaiah foretold for Egypt and Cush came some decades later, when the Assyrian kings Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal invaded Egypt in the 670s and 660s BC, took Memphis and Thebes, and carried away captives.
cultural:
Sackcloth, a coarse garment of goat hair, was worn by mourners and sometimes by prophets as a sign of grief over the people's sin. Taking it off along with his sandals, Isaiah went about naked and barefoot. The Hebrew word for naked can mean fully unclothed, but it is also used of someone stripped of the outer garment and wearing only a loincloth or undergarment, and many interpreters think that is meant here. Either way, the sign was shocking in a culture where dignity was expressed through clothing.

The image was drawn from real practice. Assyrian palace reliefs show prisoners of war being marched away stripped and barefoot, and deporting conquered peoples was standard Assyrian policy. Captives walked hundreds of miles in this state. To show Egypt and Cush, the proud southern powers, reduced to this was to show their total humiliation. Prophetic sign-acts like this were a recognized form of preaching: Jeremiah wore a yoke (Jeremiah 27), and Ezekiel lay on his side and cut his hair (Ezekiel 4 and 5).
literary: Chapter 20 is a prose narrative, unlike the poetry around it. It follows a simple pattern: a date (verse 1), God's command and Isaiah's obedience (verse 2), and God's interpretation of the sign (verses 3 to 6). The key terms sign and omen (verse 3) mark the action as a message. The interpretation turns on a double parallel: as Isaiah walks naked and barefoot, so will the captives of Egypt and Cush. The chapter ends with the voice of the dwellers of this coastland, the Philistines and their neighbors, and it closes with a question left hanging: “How then can we escape?” The answer the book will give is that there is escape only in the LORD.

outline.t: The date: Sargon's commander captures Ashdod
Isaiah removes his sackcloth and sandals
The sign explained: Egypt and Cush led away naked
Those who trusted Egypt and Cush are ashamed

doctrines.note: The chapter asks where hope is placed. Those who made Cush their hope and Egypt their boast are shamed. Trust in the strongest available human power is still misplaced trust when it replaces trust in God.
God speaks not only through words but through a prophet's actions. Isaiah's obedience made the message visible, and his costly sign shows that the messenger's own life can become part of God's word.
The rise and fall of Assyria, Egypt, and the small states between them unfold as God has spoken beforehand. History is not random; it answers to the word of the LORD.

words.note: Ot, a sign. It can be a miraculous sign, as in the exodus, or a pointer that confirms or illustrates a message, as with the rainbow or circumcision. Here Isaiah himself is the sign; compare 8:18, where he says that he and his children are signs and wonders in Israel.

Mophet, a wonder, portent, or omen. Often paired with sign, it names something striking that points beyond itself. The pairing in verse 3 presents Isaiah's three years of barefoot walking as a warning in action.

Arom, naked. It appears three times, describing both Isaiah and the captives. The same root family appears in Genesis 2:25, where the first humans were naked and unashamed. Here nakedness is the shame of defeat, the stripping of everything a person or a nation relied on.

Mabbat, expectation or hope, literally that to which one looks. In verses 5 and 6 it names Cush as the hope of the coastland peoples. The word exposes what Judah and its neighbors were looking to for salvation.

christ: The chapter's link to Christ is thematic. Isaiah embodied God's message at real personal cost, walking in shame for three years so that others might see the truth. The New Testament presents Jesus as the one in whom God's word became flesh (John 1:14), whose whole life, and especially his death, was the message. Jesus was stripped of his clothes at the crucifixion (Mark 15:24) and bore public shame, not as a sign of someone else's coming defeat but in the place of others, so that those who trust him would not be put to shame (Romans 10:11). The question of verse 6, how then can we escape, is answered in the gospel by a rescuer who did not escape.

hard.q: Did God really command Isaiah to go naked for three years?
hard.a: Readers have found this command troubling. Several points help. First, the Hebrew word for naked is used for being partly clothed as well as fully unclothed, and many interpreters think Isaiah wore only a loincloth or undergarment, which would still have been deeply humiliating. Second, the three years may describe the length of the sign's significance (the period of the Ashdod crisis) rather than continuous public nakedness; some suggest he appeared this way at intervals. Third, prophetic sign-acts were often extreme on purpose, and similar demands were made of Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Hosea. The point was to shock a complacent audience. The difficulty should not be explained away, but it fits a pattern in which God's messengers bore in their bodies the message they preached.

questions: Judah was tempted to trust Egypt and Cush against Assyria. What are the Egypts people lean on today when they feel threatened?
Isaiah obeyed a costly and embarrassing command. What would obedience to God cost you right now that you have been avoiding?
The coastland people ask, how then can we escape? How would you answer that question for someone whose hope has just collapsed?
